paragraphs: BREAD addresses a difficulty in teaching small language models to reason: expert solutions can be too hard to imitate, while independent attempts can fail too often to provide useful rewards. The paper examines the usual sequence of supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. In a simplified Markov-chain model, this sequence can fail completely when expert traces exceed the student's expressive capacity or successful attempts become exponentially rare as complexity grows.

The proposed method modifies Group Relative Policy Optimization by combining short expert prefixes with student-generated continuations. When independent attempts fail, BREAD adaptively supplies a starting hint and branches into further reasoning attempts. Its mechanism ensures that each update includes a successful trace, making rewards less sparse and creating a curriculum through partial assistance.

The authors report using fewer than 40% of ground-truth traces, consistently outperforming standard GRPO, and accelerating training by about threefold. They also find cases that BREAD solves but the supervised-then-reinforcement approach does not. These results support partial expert guidance as a way to make difficult reasoning training productive for small models.
neurips-2025-bread-branched-rollouts-fro.tldr: BREAD helps small language models learn reasoning by branching from short expert hints when independent attempts fail.

paragraphs: Language consists of discrete categories, but diffusion generation relies on progressively refining a noisy state. The paper argues that moving directly between discrete states loses signals that could help later refinement. Existing continuous approaches have nevertheless lagged behind discrete diffusion, motivating a clearer mathematical relationship between the two ways of representing the generation process.

The authors construct a continuous language diffusion model around the geometry of categorical probability distributions. They connect discrete diffusion to continuous movement on a statistical manifold, a space whose points represent distributions. This connection leads to a simple diffusion process that generalizes existing discrete models. They also introduce training that avoids simulation by exploiting radial symmetry, together with a technique for handling the manifold's high dimensionality.

Experiments on language benchmarks and other modalities show improvements over existing discrete diffusion models, with performance approaching autoregressive models. The contribution is both a modeling framework and an empirical result: preserving a continuous representation of categorical uncertainty provides an effective basis for iterative generation in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-continuous-diffusion-model-.tldr: A continuous diffusion model uses categorical-distribution geometry to outperform existing discrete diffusion methods and approach autoregressive performance.

paragraphs: Controllable image generation asks a model to follow an input such as a pose, segmentation, or depth map. ControlNet++ improves this alignment using an approximation restricted to low-noise timesteps. Preference learning over generated images offers another route, but paired images may differ in quality as well as controllability, making the intended training signal difficult to isolate.

Condition Preference Optimization changes what gets compared. It constructs preferred and disfavored control signals and trains the model to prefer the better condition. The paper presents this as removing the confounding factors in image-pair comparisons. It theoretically establishes lower contrastive-loss variance than Direct Preference Optimization and reports lower computation and storage costs for preparing training data.

Experiments show improved controllability over ControlNet++ across several control types: error reductions exceed 10% for segmentation, reach 70–80% for human pose, and fall between 2–5% for edges and depth. Here, error measures the gap between evaluated controllability and oracle results. These findings suggest that choosing cleaner preference comparisons can improve both training efficiency and control fidelity.
neurips-2025-cpo-condition-preference-op.tldr: CPO learns preferences over control signals to improve image controllability with lower training-objective variance and cheaper dataset preparation.

paragraphs: Thermal infrared images can suffer from noise, blur, and poor contrast at the same time. Methods designed for one degradation struggle with these combinations, while general enhancement methods developed for RGB images do not transfer cleanly because thermal cameras form images differently. The paper therefore builds its enhancement approach around the thermal imaging process.

Its Recurrent Prompt Fusion Network creates pairs of prompts associated with different degradations. The corresponding prompts are combined to adjust internal model features, supplying guidance for both individual problems and mixtures. A selective recurrent training mechanism progressively improves how the network handles composite degradation, supporting noise removal while retaining structural detail and increasing contrast.

The work also introduces an infrared benchmark covering a broad range of scenarios. Experiments report promising visual results for individual degradations and an 8.76% performance improvement on complex degradation scenes. The central contribution is an enhancement system that explicitly coordinates multiple kinds of correction, supported by a benchmark intended to evaluate infrared enhancement across varied conditions.
neurips-2025-enhancing-infrared-vision-p.tldr: A thermal-imaging-informed prompt network improves infrared images affected by combined degradations, alongside a new evaluation benchmark.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can struggle to recognize inputs that differ from their training distribution. Energy-based detectors try to identify these inputs using the model's class scores. This paper finds that their reliability is undermined by a coupling between the magnitude and direction of node representations, which leads to systematic mistakes on unfamiliar samples with large representation norms.

The proposed GeoEnergy framework builds on another property of graph networks: representations belonging to the same class tend to point in similar directions. It normalizes class weights while retaining the lengths of node representations, enforcing a hyperspherical geometry for the class scores. This separation produces more structured energy distributions, tighter directional alignment within classes, and better calibration.

GeoEnergy can be added to existing energy-based graph networks without retraining or changing their architecture. Across the evaluated benchmarks and distribution shifts, it consistently improves detection and confidence reliability. The results show that the geometry used to turn representations into scores can materially affect uncertainty detection, even without learning an entirely new graph model.
neurips-2025-geometric-logit-decoupling-.tldr: GeoEnergy improves graph out-of-distribution detection by restructuring class-score geometry without retraining the network.

paragraphs: HoliGS reconstructs dynamic environments from long videos recorded by a single RGB camera, then renders them from new viewpoints. The target is embodied view synthesis, where cameras may follow actors or move through a scene from an egocentric perspective. Existing dynamic reconstruction pipelines face substantial training overhead on minute-long recordings, particularly when scenes contain movement and changing viewpoints.

The framework separates a scene into a static background and moving objects represented by learned Gaussian primitives. Object motion is organized into global rigid movement, skeleton-based articulation, and smaller non-rigid deformation through an invertible neural flow. Attaching these primitives to a complete canonical foreground shape supports rendering across substantial viewpoint changes and interactions among multiple actors.

Experiments report better reconstruction quality and substantially shorter training and rendering times than leading monocular deformable NeRF methods. The hierarchical motion representation is central to this result: it provides a structured way to combine different forms of movement while supporting flexible viewing trajectories. The findings position HoliGS as a practical approach to longer, dynamic embodied captures.
neurips-2025-holigs-holistic-gaussian-sp.tldr: HoliGS uses hierarchical Gaussian deformation to reconstruct long dynamic monocular videos and efficiently render new embodied viewpoints.

paragraphs: Inverse problems recover an unknown object from measurements that may be incomplete or noisy. This paper asks how many measurements suffice when recovery uses posterior sampling with an approximate prior. It develops high-probability guarantees for stable, accurate recovery while allowing general distributions for the prior, measurement operator, and noise.

The main finite-sample bound depends on two ingredients. One is the approximate covering number of the prior, which measures its intrinsic complexity through how economically its possibilities can be represented. The other is how strongly the measurement operator and noise concentrate. Together, these quantities connect the structure of plausible answers with the reliability of the measurements.

For priors produced by mapping latent variables through a deep neural network, the sufficient sample complexity scales log-linearly with latent dimension. For random sampling through an orthogonal matrix, the analysis also identifies coherence with the prior's support as a governing quantity. These are sufficient recovery guarantees under the framework's conditions, extending the role of structure and coherence into Bayesian reconstruction.
neurips-2025-how-many-measurements-are-e.tldr: The paper derives sufficient measurement bounds for Bayesian recovery using prior complexity and concentration properties of measurements and noise.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses where to evaluate an unknown function while trying to keep the accumulated cost of suboptimal choices small. This paper studies the Bayesian setting in which that function is drawn from a known Gaussian process. Its focus is the regret guarantee for Gaussian Process Upper Confidence Bound, or GP-UCB.

Under a Matérn kernel with the required degree of smoothness, the authors establish a high-probability cumulative-regret bound of approximately square-root growth in the number of evaluations, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Under a squared exponential kernel, they obtain a bound of O(√(T ln² T)). These results close the stated gap between the existing GP-UCB upper bound and the best comparison upper bound.

The improvement comes from analyzing how the sequence of inputs actually selected by GP-UCB concentrates. This allows a more refined treatment of the Gaussian process's information gain. The contribution is therefore a sharper analysis of an established algorithm: under the stated probabilistic model and kernel conditions, its accumulated regret grows more slowly than earlier guarantees showed.
neurips-2025-improved-regret-bounds-for-.tldr: A refined analysis gives GP-UCB stronger cumulative-regret guarantees under specified Gaussian-process kernels.

paragraphs: Secure multi-party computation provides formal data privacy for language-model inference, but its latency becomes especially costly with long inputs. Techniques that reduce attention work in ordinary inference do not directly deliver the same benefits in this setting. MPCache therefore designs cache reduction around the computational demands of private inference itself.

The framework uses two stages based on the observation that past tokens contribute differently to later generation. A one-time static pass discards unimportant key-value cache entries. A dynamic stage then uses the current query to select a small subset of the remaining cache for attention. Similarity approximations suited to secure computation, hierarchical cache clustering, and index sharing across layers further reduce selection costs.

Across the tested generation tasks, MPCache consistently outperforms previous cache-eviction baselines. Depending on sequence length, it reports decoding-latency reductions by factors of 1.8–2.01 and communication reductions by factors of 3.39–8.37. The results illustrate why efficient private inference requires attention-selection mechanisms designed for secure computation, including the expense of selecting which cached information to use.
neurips-2025-mpcache-mpc-friendly-kv-cac.tldr: MPCache combines static cache eviction and query-aware selection to reduce private language-model inference latency and communication.

paragraphs: Whole-slide classification combines information from many image patches to predict a label for an entire slide. The paper revisits simple multiple-instance learning because Transformer approaches often offer only modest gains when training data are scarce. It focuses on how patch evidence is pooled, using unsupervised slide features without attention.

The authors analyze temperature-controlled log-sum-exp pooling. For a slide with N patches, they establish a smooth transition near a critical temperature parameter of order log N. On one side, pooling behaves more like an average, favoring stability and generalization; on the other, it behaves more like a maximum, increasing sensitivity but loosening generalization bounds. Maxsoft provides flexible control over this trade-off.

The paper also introduces PerPatch augmentation to improve robustness to specimen heterogeneity. Across four named benchmarks, Maxsoft achieves state-of-the-art results in low-data settings and often matches or exceeds large foundation models. PerPatch further improves performance. These findings emphasize the practical value of controlling evidence aggregation when data availability constrains the benefit of more elaborate architectures.
neurips-2025-navigating-the-mil-trade-of.tldr: Maxsoft adjusts the sensitivity–generalization trade-off in slide pooling and achieves strong whole-slide classification with limited training data.

paragraphs: One-step generators can produce high-quality content efficiently, but adding a new control condition can require expensive changes to a diffusion model followed by another distillation process. Noise Consistency Training instead adapts a pretrained one-step generator directly. It needs neither the original training images nor retraining of the underlying diffusion model.

NCT adds an adapter and trains it with a consistency objective in the generator's noise space. The objective aligns generation behavior across noises with different degrees of conditional dependence, implicitly encouraging adherence to the desired control. The authors interpret this through moment matching: the adapted generator is aligned with a difficult-to-compute conditional distribution defined jointly by the generator and a discriminative control model.

The method requires only the pretrained generator and a control-signal model, making the adaptation modular and data-efficient. Experiments report state-of-the-art controllable generation in a single forward pass, exceeding evaluated multi-step and distillation-based methods in quality and computational efficiency. The findings support adding controls through an auxiliary training objective while retaining the generator's one-step execution.
neurips-2025-noise-consistency-training-.tldr: Noise Consistency Training adds new controls to pretrained one-step generators using an adapter and a noise-space consistency objective.

paragraphs: Reading text in an image involves more than recognizing words. A model may also need to locate text, extract handwriting, understand layout, and reason about what it reads. OCRBench v2 broadens evaluation toward these harder abilities, which the authors identify as underexplored despite strong results on existing text-recognition benchmarks.

The bilingual benchmark contains 10,000 human-verified question-answer pairs across 31 scenarios, with a high proportion of difficult examples. It covers four times as many tasks as the earlier OCRBench and supplies evaluation metrics for this broader scope. The authors also create a private test set containing 1,500 manually annotated images. Similar evaluation trends on the public and private sets support the benchmark's reliability.

Most evaluated multimodal models score below 50 out of 100. The analysis identifies weaknesses in uncommon text recognition, fine-grained perception, layout understanding, complex-element parsing, and logical reasoning. These results show that strong text recognition does not by itself establish competence across the wider range of visual-text tasks measured by the benchmark.
neurips-2025-ocrbench-v2-an-improved-ben.tldr: OCRBench v2 expands visual-text evaluation and reveals substantial weaknesses in multimodal models' localization, perception, and reasoning.

paragraphs: The same language-model response can carry different risks for different people. This paper studies personalized safety: whether an answer is appropriate given a user's background or condition. It argues that evaluations centered on context-independent properties, such as factuality or toxicity, miss this dependence on individual vulnerability in sensitive applications.

The authors introduce PENGUIN, a benchmark containing 14,000 scenarios across seven sensitive domains. Each scenario has variants with and without user context. Testing six leading models, they report that supplying personalized information improves safety scores by 43.2%. The analysis also finds that some context attributes contribute more than others, motivating selective information gathering.

RAISE implements that idea through a training-free, two-stage agent that strategically acquires user background. It improves safety scores by up to 31.6% over six unmodified models while asking an average of 2.7 questions. These benchmark results support targeted context collection as a practical way to improve personalized responses without retraining, with reported benefits expressed in safety scores rather than a guarantee of harmlessness.
neurips-2025-personalized-safety-in-llms.tldr: PENGUIN measures user-dependent safety, while RAISE improves benchmark safety scores by selectively asking for relevant personal context.

paragraphs: A neural network's uncertainty estimates can become unreliable when deployment inputs differ from its training data. This paper focuses on covariate shift, including changes caused by selection bias or variation over time. Its goal is to make uncertainty estimates account explicitly for those input differences, particularly where predictive performance is likely to deteriorate.

The proposed Bayesian framework uses a prior conditioned on both the training covariates and the new covariates. Rather than keeping the prior fixed, this construction naturally raises uncertainty for inputs far from the training distribution. Amortized variational inference efficiently approximates the resulting predictive distribution. The method also creates synthetic environments using small bootstrap samples from the original training set to simulate plausible shifts.

Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets report substantially better uncertainty estimates under distribution shift than existing approaches. The contribution is a coordinated way to represent unfamiliarity in the prior and approximate its predictive consequences efficiently. The simulated environments provide varied shift conditions using the original dataset, supporting the framework without requiring a separate dataset for each possible shift.
neurips-2025-quantifying-uncertainty-in-.tldr: An adaptive Bayesian prior uses training and deployment inputs to improve uncertainty estimates under covariate shift.

paragraphs: RAPID Hand addresses the shortage of affordable platforms for collecting dexterous robot-manipulation demonstrations. A hand with many controllable motions is useful only if operators can guide it accurately and its sensors capture dependable data. The paper therefore designs the hand, perception system, and teleoperation interface together.

The platform combines a compact 20-degree-of-freedom hand with wrist-mounted vision, fingertip touch sensing, and proprioception. Its hardware-level perception framework integrates these signals with spatial alignment and latency below seven milliseconds. A universal actuation scheme, custom perception electronics, and two retargeting constraints support the joint design, addressing precision and stability challenges in controlling a complex multi-fingered hand.

The authors evaluate the hardware, sensing, and teleoperation interface, then train a diffusion policy on the collected demonstrations. The policy outperforms prior work in their evaluation, supporting the platform's ability to collect useful, high-quality data. Built from inexpensive, off-the-shelf components, RAPID Hand is intended for public release to improve reproducibility and adoption. Its contribution centers on making dexterous demonstration collection more accessible as an integrated system.
neurips-2025-rapid-hand-robust-affordabl.tldr: RAPID Hand jointly designs an affordable dexterous hand, integrated sensing, and teleoperation for reliable robot-demonstration collection.

paragraphs: Image-editing systems can use visual examples to communicate a desired change, but methods based on a single reference image tend to focus on style or appearance and struggle with non-rigid transformations. This paper instead uses a source image together with its edited target. The pair supplies evidence about the editing relationship that should be transferred to another image.

RelationAdapter is a lightweight module for Diffusion Transformer models that extracts this content-aware editing intent from minimal examples and applies it to a new query image. Inspired by in-context learning in language models, the approach makes the transformation illustrated by the pair central to the visual prompt. It targets the ability to capture and reuse editing relationships across image content.

The authors also introduce Relation252K, a dataset spanning 218 editing tasks for evaluating generalization and adaptability. Experiments on this dataset show substantial improvements in understanding and transferring editing intent, alongside better generation quality and overall editing performance. The results support paired visual demonstrations as useful guidance for a broader range of image transformations.
neurips-2025-relationadapter-learning-an.tldr: RelationAdapter learns an editing relationship from source–target image pairs and transfers it to new images.

paragraphs: Scalable oversight asks whether weaker AI systems can supervise stronger ones. This paper models the probability of success as a function of both systems' capabilities. Oversight becomes a game between unequal players, whose task-specific Elo scores vary piecewise linearly with general capability, with plateaus for task incompetence and task saturation.

The authors validate the framework using modified Nim and study four oversight games: Mafia, Debate, Backdoor Code, and Wargames. They find scaling relationships that approximate performance in each domain. They then analyze nested oversight, where trusted models supervise stronger untrusted models, which become trusted supervisors at the next level. The analysis identifies conditions for success and computes the number of levels that maximizes success probability.

Applying the theory at a general Elo gap of 400 gives nested-oversight success rates of 13.5% for Mafia, 51.7% for Debate, 10.0% for Backdoor Code, and 9.4% for Wargames. Rates fall further for stronger targets. These results show substantial dependence on the oversight task and capability gap, rather than establishing that additional supervision levels reliably overcome capability differences.
neurips-2025-scaling-laws-for-scalable-o.tldr: A game-based framework models oversight scaling and identifies when chains of increasingly capable supervisors can succeed.

paragraphs: Video diffusion Transformers spend substantial time on attention, whose cost grows quadratically with token count. Sparse attention reduces this work by selecting important tokens. The paper identifies two obstacles: grouping tokens by position can obscure which ones matter, and scattering important tokens among irrelevant ones wastes computation on GPUs that favor contiguous data.

Sparse VideoGen2 addresses both through semantic-aware permutation. It uses k-means to group tokens by semantic similarity, then reorders them. The resulting groups provide more accurate aggregate representations for selecting important tokens and place selected work into a denser layout that avoids padding. Dynamic Top-p budget control and custom kernels further support efficient execution, without additional model training.

The authors report speedups of up to 2.30 times on HunyuanVideo and 1.89 times on Wan 2.1, with reported PSNR values up to 30 and 26, respectively. The framework improves the quality–efficiency trade-off in their evaluation. Its central insight is that effective sparse attention requires both accurate token selection and a memory layout that lets hardware exploit that selection.
neurips-2025-sparse-videogen2-accelerate.tldr: Sparse VideoGen2 clusters and reorders semantically similar tokens to make sparse video attention more accurate and GPU-efficient without training.

paragraphs: Coreset selection seeks a small training subset that preserves the benefits of using the full dataset. Gradient-based selection has strong motivations, but a subset's representativeness can deteriorate as training progresses and its loss curvature diverges from that of the full data. The paper also notes that ordinary stochastic gradient descent is a surprisingly competitive baseline.

The proposed framework connects posterior sampling with loss landscapes to make subset selection more robust, including when data corruption is high. It also smooths the loss using posterior sampling over model weights. This smoothing is intended to improve stability and generalization while preserving computational efficiency, addressing how the selected subset behaves over the course of optimization.

The authors provide a convergence analysis for their sampling-based selection method. Experiments across diverse datasets report faster training and better generalization than the current state of the art. The contribution is therefore more than choosing representative examples at one point: it uses sampling and loss smoothing to support a more stable relationship between subset training and the full-data objective.
neurips-2025-stable-coresets-via-posteri.tldr: Posterior sampling and loss smoothing make coreset selection more stable, with reported improvements in training speed and generalization.

paragraphs: When workers can value multiple jobs equally, stable matching no longer offers a single outcome that maximizes every worker's utility. The paper introduces the Optimal Stable Share ratio to measure this conflict. It compares a worker's best utility across stable matchings with the utility that worker receives in a particular matching.

The authors prove that randomizing only over stable matchings can still produce utility losses growing linearly with the number of workers. Allowing possibly unstable matchings changes the achievable guarantee: their efficient algorithm computes a distribution with an asymptotically tight logarithmic ratio. A second algorithm handles unknown exact utilities, providing a logarithmic utility approximation while keeping instability bounded.

The paper then extends the analysis to bandit learning, where utilities are observed only for pairs that are actually matched. An adaptive algorithm bridges strict preferences and statistical ties using worker-optimal stable regret. A lower bound exposes a fundamental trade-off between those regimes. Together, the results quantify how utility protection, stability, and incomplete information interact when preferences contain ties.
neurips-2025-stable-matching-with-ties-a.tldr: Allowing controlled departures from stable matching enables much stronger worker-utility guarantees in markets with tied preferences.

paragraphs: Training software-engineering agents requires tasks and execution environments in which their solutions can be checked. The paper identifies data collection as a major bottleneck: earlier datasets contain at most thousands of examples from relatively few repositories, while curation can require hundreds of human hours and substantial storage for execution environments.

SWE-smith automates this process for Python codebases. It builds an execution environment and synthesizes hundreds to thousands of task instances that cause existing tests to fail. Using this pipeline, the authors create 50,000 examples from 128 GitHub repositories, reporting an order-of-magnitude increase over prior work. Existing tests provide the basis for constructing these executable training problems.

Training SWE-agent-LM-32B with this effort yields a 40.2% Pass@1 resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified, reported as state of the art among open-source models. The authors release the collection procedure, tasks, trajectories, and models. The contribution links scalable task generation with a demonstrated agent-training result, while making the components available for further software-engineering research.
neurips-2025-swe-smith-scaling-data-for-.tldr: SWE-smith automatically creates executable software-repair training tasks at scale and supports a strong open-source coding agent.

paragraphs: Debugging a real SQL issue requires capabilities beyond translating a request into a query. BIRD-CRITIC evaluates this problem using 530 PostgreSQL tasks and 570 multi-dialect tasks derived from authentic user issues and replayed in new environments. Baseline results show the difficulty: O3-Mini achieves success rates of 38.87% and 33.33% on the two sets.

The paper also introduces Six-Gym to train open-source models for SQL debugging. Its SQL-Rewind strategy works backward from verified SQL to generate executable issue–solution data. A further method, f-Plan Boosting, extracts high-level debugging plans from solutions. These plans help teacher models produce 73.7% more successful training trajectories, drawing additional supervision from the available solutions.

The resulting BIRD-Fixer agent, based on Qwen-2.5-Coder-14B, reaches 38.11% success on the PostgreSQL set and 29.65% on the multi-dialect set. It exceeds several proprietary models, including the named Claude and GPT comparisons. The work combines a realistic evaluation target with a data-generation and training process that improves access to capable open-source SQL debugging.
neurips-2025-swe-sql-illuminating-llm-pa.tldr: BIRD-CRITIC benchmarks real SQL debugging, while Six-Gym and plan-based training support the competitive open-source BIRD-Fixer agent.

paragraphs: Some network architectures perform poorly on particular tasks despite hyperparameter tuning: they may overfit, underfit, or converge to weak solutions. This paper investigates whether useful inductive biases can be transferred from another architecture while retaining the target network. It calls the transfer mechanism guidance.

A frozen guide network steers the target through a neural distance function. Training combines the ordinary task objective with layerwise representational similarity to the guide. A trained guide transfers both learned knowledge and architectural prior; an untrained guide transfers only part of its architectural prior. This distinction lets the method examine how architecture itself can shape another network's learning.

The experiments show guidance preventing fully connected network overfitting on ImageNet, narrowing the vanilla RNN–Transformer gap, improving plain CNNs toward ResNet accuracy, and helping Transformers on tasks favoring RNNs. Guidance-based initialization alone can also mitigate fully connected network overfitting. These findings support representational alignment as a training tool and a way to investigate architectural priors; automating architecture design remains a possible longer-term use.
neurips-2025-training-the-untrainable-in.tldr: Aligning a target network's representations with a frozen guide can transfer useful architectural biases and improve otherwise poor training outcomes.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning trains a shared graph model from distributed data. Without labels, local models can develop incompatible representation spaces because they lack shared semantic guidance. Simply combining their parameters through conventional weighted aggregation can also degrade the global model. FedPAM addresses these two problems with separate but coordinated modules.

Representation Space Alignment uses learnable anchors to define a common global space. It aligns local subgraphs to those anchors through fused Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport. Adaptive Global Parameter Learning then stacks local model parameters into third-order tensors and combines them within a low-rank tensor space, allowing the global update to incorporate higher-order relationships among clients.

Experiments on eight graph datasets show that FedPAM outperforms the classical and state-of-the-art methods included in the comparison. The design highlights two distinct requirements for unsupervised federation: local representations need a shared reference, and global parameter integration needs to account for relationships among the local models. The reported results support addressing both when building a global graph network without training labels.
neurips-2025-unsupervised-federated-grap.tldr: FedPAM aligns unlabeled graph representations across clients and adaptively combines their parameters to improve federated graph learning.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models connect visual observations and language with robot actions. Their usual supervised fine-tuning can leave them vulnerable to compounding errors when conditions change. This paper investigates how reinforcement learning, which optimizes task objectives through trial and error, changes their generalization compared with supervised training.

The authors introduce a benchmark that separates visual, semantic, and execution dimensions of generalization. This separation makes it possible to ask which abilities benefit from reinforcement learning rather than treating robustness as a single outcome. Their experiments compare reinforcement-learning approaches and find that PPO is more effective for these models than language-model-derived methods such as DPO and GRPO.

PPO fine-tuning substantially improves semantic understanding and execution robustness over supervised fine-tuning, while visual robustness remains comparable. The authors also provide a simple recipe for efficient PPO training and demonstrate its usefulness. The findings support reinforcement learning as a practical tool for particular forms of VLA generalization, with the observed gains concentrated in semantic and execution behavior rather than an improvement across every tested dimension.
neurips-2025-what-can-rl-bring-to-vla-ge.tldr: PPO fine-tuning improves VLA semantic generalization and execution robustness over supervised training while maintaining comparable visual robustness.
